SB 9 TWO-UNIT HOUSING DEVELOPMENT AND URBAN LOT SPLIT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814

SB 9 TWO-UNIT DEVELOPMENT / URBAN LOT SPLIT — PROJECT IDENTIFICATION
SB 9 TWO-UNIT HOUSING DEVELOPMENT / URBAN LOT SPLIT — PROJECT INFORMATION
(Referencing California Government Code sections 65852.21 (two-unit housing developments) and 66411.7 (urban lot splits), governing ministerial local-agency approval of certain housing on single-family-zoned parcels)

Property Owner: Jordan Lee
Property Address: 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814
Assessor's Parcel Number: 123-456-789
Local Agency (city, county, or city and county with permitting jurisdiction over the property): City of Sacramento

Type of Application (check one or both): ___ Two-unit housing development under Government Code section 65852.21 ___ Urban lot split under Government Code section 66411.7

Date Application Submitted to Local Agency: _______________________________________________

This sheet identifies the property, the owner, and the local agency for reference in connection with a two-unit housing development or urban lot split application. It states facts for identification purposes only; it does not itself constitute or substitute for the application that must be submitted to, and acted on by, the local agency, and it does not determine whether the proposed development or lot split qualifies for ministerial approval under any particular provision of Government Code section 65852.21 or 66411.7.

MINISTERIAL APPROVAL OF A TWO-UNIT HOUSING DEVELOPMENT
California law requires a local agency to consider a proposed housing development containing no more than two residential units within a single-family residential zone ministerially -- without discretionary review or a hearing -- if the development meets a defined set of statutory requirements. One of those requirements is a location condition: the parcel must be located within a city whose boundaries include some portion of an urbanized area or urban cluster (as the United States Census Bureau designates those areas), or, for an unincorporated area, the parcel must lie wholly within the boundaries of such an urbanized area or urban cluster. A separate requirement cross-references specific parcel-eligibility criteria drawn from a different housing-streamlining statute (Government Code section 65913.4, as it read on September 16, 2021).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A proposed housing development containing no more than two residential units within a single-family residential zone shall be considered ministerially, without discretionary review or a hearing, if the proposed housing development meets all of the following requirements:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(a) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  "The parcel subject to the proposed housing development is located within a city, the boundaries of which include some portion of either an urbanized area or urban cluster, as designated by the United States Census Bureau, or, for unincorporated areas, a legal parcel wholly within the boundaries of an urbanized area or urban cluster, as designated by the United States Census Bureau."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 65852.21(a), as currently in effect (most recently amended by Stats. 2026, ch. 56 (SB 1426), effective June 30, 2026). This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law currently requires for ministerial approval of a two-unit development -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel, and most states have no comparable statewide ministerial-approval mandate for splitting a single-family lot's zoning capacity into two units. This clause states only the ministerial-review mandate and the urbanized-area location requirement; the parcel's other eligibility conditions (protected-housing and historic-property exclusions) are addressed in a separate clause of this document, and the cross-referenced eligibility criteria from Government Code section 65913.4(a)(6)(B)-(K) are not independently restated or verified here. This clause does not determine whether a specific parcel in fact lies within an urbanized area or urban cluster as the Census Bureau defines those terms, or whether a specific proposed development in fact contains no more than two residential units within the statute's own counting rule.

HOUSING EXCLUDED FROM TWO-UNIT DEVELOPMENT ELIGIBILITY
California law excludes certain categories of existing housing from eligibility for the two-unit ministerial-approval pathway. Notwithstanding any provision of the statute or any local law, the proposed development may not require demolition or alteration of housing subject to a recorded covenant, ordinance, or law restricting rents to levels affordable to moderate-, low-, or very-low-income persons and families; housing subject to any form of rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police power; or housing that has been occupied by a tenant within the last three years. Separately, the parcel is ineligible if its owner has exercised rights under the Ellis Act (Government Code section 7060 et seq.) to withdraw residential accommodations from rent or lease within the 15 years before the development proponent submits its application. The development is also ineligible if it is located in a contributing structure within a historic district on the State Historic Resources Inventory (or a historic property or district under a city or county ordinance), or on a parcel individually listed as a historical resource on that inventory or individually designated as a city or county landmark.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Notwithstanding any provision of this section or any local law, the proposed housing development would not require demolition or alteration of any of the following types of housing:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  "Housing that has been occupied by a tenant in the last three years."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(a)(3)(C) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(a)(3)(C) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  "The parcel subject to the proposed housing development is not a parcel on which an owner of residential real property has exercised the owner’s rights under Chapter 12.75 (commencing with Section 7060) of Division 7 of Title 1 to withdraw accommodations from rent or lease within 15 years before the date that the development proponent submits an application."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(a)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  "A contributing structure within a historic district included on the State Historic Resources Inventory, as defined in Section 5020.1 of the Public Resources Code, or historic property or district pursuant to a city or county ordinance."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(a)(5)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(a)(5)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 65852.21(a)(3)-(5), as currently in effect. It is one state's statute; the categories described here (rent-restricted housing, recently tenant-occupied housing, Ellis Act withdrawals, and historic resources) are specific to this California statute's own eligibility scheme and do not describe a generally applicable rule. The four citations below are each independent subdivisions of the same statutory subsection (a) rather than independently authored sources. This clause does not determine whether a specific unit is in fact rent-restricted, has in fact been tenant-occupied within the last three years, is on a parcel where Ellis Act rights were in fact exercised within the 15-year window, or is in fact within a listed historic district or on a landmark parcel -- those are fact-specific determinations a local agency and its records would resolve.

LIMITS ON LOCAL DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS FOR A TWO-UNIT DEVELOPMENT
A local agency may impose objective zoning, subdivision, and design-review standards on a two-unit development that do not conflict with the statute, but those standards may not have the effect of physically precluding construction of up to two units, or of precluding either unit from being at least 800 square feet in floor area. On setbacks, no setback may be required at all for an existing structure, or for a structure built in the same location and to the same dimensions as an existing structure; in other circumstances, a local agency may require a setback of up to four feet from the side and rear lot lines.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The local agency shall not impose objective zoning standards, objective subdivision standards, and objective design standards that would have the effect of physically precluding the construction of up to two units or that would physically preclude either of the two units from being at least 800 square feet in floor area."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(b)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(b)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  "Notwithstanding subparagraph (A), in all other circumstances not described in clause (i), a local agency may require a setback of up to four feet from the side and rear lot lines."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(b)(2)(B)(ii) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(b)(2)(B)(ii) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 65852.21(b)(1)-(2), as currently in effect. It is one state's statute, describing the ceiling this particular statute places on local development standards for this particular ministerial pathway -- not a general rule about zoning standards, and not a claim about what standards apply outside this pathway. One quoted passage below (the setback rule) is drawn from source text in which the HTML places a line-wrap between the words "local" and "agency"; that mid-word line-wrap whitespace is a source-formatting artifact and has been normalized to a single space in the quotation below, not a substantive correction. This clause does not address the statute's separate rules on offstreet parking (a separate clause of this document) or its rule permitting a local agency to adopt standards preserving a historic district's historical value, and it does not determine whether a specific local ordinance's standards in fact comply with these limits.

PARKING LIMITS, REVIEW TIMELINE, AND HEALTH/SAFETY DENIAL FOR A TWO-UNIT DEVELOPMENT
In addition to development standards, a local agency may require offstreet parking of up to one space per unit for a two-unit development, except that no parking may be required if the parcel is within one-half mile walking distance of a high-quality transit corridor or a major transit stop, or if a car-share vehicle is located within one block of the parcel. An application for a two-unit development must be considered and approved or denied within 60 days of the local agency's receipt of a completed application; if the local agency does not act within that period, the application is deemed approved. Notwithstanding the ministerial-approval mandate, a local agency may still deny a proposed development if the building official makes a written finding, based on a preponderance of the evidence, that the development would have a specific, adverse impact on public health and safety, as that term is defined in a separate housing-streamlining statute (Government Code section 65589.5(d)(2)), for which there is no feasible way to satisfactorily mitigate or avoid the impact.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Offstreet parking of up to one space per unit, except that a local agency shall not impose parking requirements in either of the following instances:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  "60 days from the date the local agency receives a completed application. If the local agency has not approved or denied the completed application within 60 days, the application shall be deemed approved."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(h)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(h)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 65852.21(c)(1), (d), and (h)(1), as currently in effect. It is one state's statute. The health/safety denial ground incorporates by cross-reference a definition found in a separate statute (Government Code section 65589.5(d)(2)) that this clause does not independently restate or verify; the body describes that cross-reference but the citation below covers only the deemed-approval timeline and the parking cap, which are this clause's directly quoted, independently verified statutory text. This clause does not address the separate percolation-test condition the statute allows for units on an onsite wastewater treatment system, and it does not determine whether a specific denial finding would in fact satisfy the statute's preponderance-of-the-evidence and no-feasible-mitigation standard.

MINIMUM RENTAL TERM AND INTERACTION WITH ADU/JADU AUTHORITY
A local agency must require that a rental of any unit created under the two-unit development statute be for a term longer than 30 days -- meaning the statute itself forecloses using a unit created under this pathway as a short-term rental of 30 days or less. Separately, if a parcel uses both this two-unit-development authority and the urban-lot-split authority (Government Code section 66411.7) together, a local agency is not required to also permit an accessory dwelling unit or junior accessory dwelling unit on that parcel, notwithstanding the statutes that otherwise govern ADU and JADU approval.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A local agency shall require that a rental of any unit created pursuant to this section be for a term longer than 30 days."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(e) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  "a local agency shall not be required to permit an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit on parcels that use both the authority contained within this section and the authority contained in Section 66411.7."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(f) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 65852.21(e) and (f), as currently in effect. It is one state's statute. This clause states the 30-day minimum rental term and the ADU/JADU-restriction-when-combined rule as written; it does not address any additional local short-term-rental ordinance that might independently apply, and it does not determine whether a specific parcel is in fact using both authorities together in a way that triggers the ADU/JADU restriction.

MINISTERIAL APPROVAL AND BASIC REQUIREMENTS FOR AN URBAN LOT SPLIT
California law requires a local agency to ministerially approve, without discretionary review, a parcel map for an urban lot split if the map meets a defined set of statutory requirements. The parcel map must subdivide an existing parcel into no more than two new parcels of approximately equal lot area, with neither resulting parcel smaller than 40 percent of the original parcel's lot area, and both resulting parcels must be no smaller than 1,200 square feet, unless a local agency has adopted an ordinance permitting a smaller minimum lot size. The parcel being subdivided must be located within a single-family residential zone and, as with a two-unit development, within a city whose boundaries include some portion of an urbanized area or urban cluster (or, for an unincorporated area, wholly within such an area) as the United States Census Bureau designates it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "a local agency shall ministerially approve, as set forth in this section, a parcel map for an urban lot split only if the local agency determines that the parcel map for the urban lot split meets all the following requirements:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(a) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "subdivides an existing parcel to create no more than two new parcels of approximately equal lot area provided that one parcel shall not be smaller than 40 percent of the lot area of the original parcel proposed for subdivision."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "both newly created parcels are no smaller than 1,200 square feet."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(a)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "The parcel is located within a single-family residential zone."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(a)(3)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66411.7(a)(1)-(3)(B) and (b)(1)(A), as currently in effect (most recently amended by Stats. 2026, ch. 56 (SB 1426), effective June 30, 2026). It is one state's statute. This clause covers the lot-count, lot-area, minimum-lot-size, zoning, and location requirements; the parcel's other eligibility conditions (protected-housing, historic-property, and prior-use exclusions) are addressed in a separate clause of this document, and the cross-referenced eligibility criteria the statute borrows from Government Code section 65913.4(a)(6)(B)-(K) are not independently restated or verified here. This clause does not determine whether a specific proposed subdivision in fact satisfies the approximately-equal-area and 40-percent minimum-share requirements, or whether a specific local agency has in fact adopted an ordinance permitting a smaller minimum lot size.

PARCELS EXCLUDED FROM URBAN LOT SPLIT ELIGIBILITY
As with the two-unit development pathway, an urban lot split is ineligible if it would require demolition or alteration of rent-restricted or rent-controlled housing, of housing on a parcel where Ellis Act rights were exercised to withdraw accommodations within the preceding 15 years, or of housing that has been occupied by a tenant within the last three years. Beyond those shared exclusions, the urban-lot-split statute adds a use-once limitation specific to this pathway: a parcel that has already been created through a prior urban lot split may not be split again, and an owner (or someone acting in concert with the owner) who has already used an urban lot split to subdivide one parcel may not use the authority again to subdivide an adjacent parcel.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Housing that has been occupied by a tenant in the last three years."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(a)(3)(D)(iv) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(a)(3)(D)(iv) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "The parcel has not been established through prior exercise of an urban lot split as provided for in this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(a)(3)(G) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(a)(3)(G) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "Neither the owner of the parcel being subdivided nor any person acting in concert with the owner has previously subdivided an adjacent parcel using an urban lot split as provided for in this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(a)(3)(H) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(a)(3)(H) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66411.7(a)(3)(D)(iii)-(iv), (G), and (H), as currently in effect. It is one state's statute. This clause does not restate the parallel historic-property exclusions in section 66411.7(a)(3)(E)-(F), which track the two-unit-development historic-property exclusions already described in a separate clause of this document, in order to avoid duplicating that content. It does not determine whether a specific parcel was in fact previously created through, or previously used in, an urban lot split, or whether a specific prior subdivision by a related owner in fact falls within the adjacent-parcel restriction.

OWNER-OCCUPANCY AFFIDAVIT REQUIREMENT FOR AN URBAN LOT SPLIT
A local agency must require an applicant for an urban lot split to sign an affidavit stating that the applicant intends to occupy one of the housing units as their principal residence for a minimum of three years from the date the urban lot split is approved. That requirement does not apply to an applicant that is a "community land trust," as a separate Revenue and Taxation Code provision defines that term, or that is a "qualified nonprofit corporation" as described in a separate Revenue and Taxation Code section. Beyond this specific affidavit requirement, a local agency may not impose any additional owner-occupancy standard on an urban lot split.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "shall require an applicant for an urban lot split to sign an affidavit stating that the applicant intends to occupy one of the housing units as their principal residence for a minimum of three years from the date of the approval of the urban lot split."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(g)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "shall not impose additional owner occupancy standards, other than provided for in this subdivision, on an urban lot split pursuant to this"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(g)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(g)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66411.7(g), as currently in effect. It is one state's statute. This clause does not independently restate or verify the cross-referenced Revenue and Taxation Code definitions of "community land trust" or "qualified nonprofit corporation"; it states only that such applicants are exempted from the affidavit requirement. This clause does not determine whether a specific applicant in fact qualifies for either exemption, or whether a specific applicant's stated intent to occupy a unit would in fact be enforceable or verified by the local agency beyond the affidavit itself.

DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS, APPROVAL TIMELINE, AND TWO-UNIT-PER-PARCEL CAP FOR AN URBAN LOT SPLIT
As with a two-unit development, a local agency may impose objective zoning, subdivision, and design-review standards on parcels created by an urban lot split, but those standards may not have the effect of physically precluding construction of two units on either resulting parcel, or result in a unit smaller than 800 square feet; no setback is required for an existing structure or one rebuilt in the same location and dimensions, and otherwise a local agency may require a setback of up to four feet from the side and rear lot lines. A local agency may not impose regulations requiring dedication of rights-of-way or construction of offsite improvements as a condition of an urban-lot-split parcel map, and it may not require correction of nonconforming zoning conditions as a condition of ministerial approval. An application for an urban lot split must be approved or denied within 60 days of a completed application being received, with deemed approval if the local agency misses that deadline. A local agency must also require that a rental of any unit created under this section be for a term longer than 30 days. Finally, notwithstanding several other statutes governing two-unit developments, density bonuses, and accessory dwelling units, a local agency is not required to permit more than two units on a parcel created through an urban lot split.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A local agency shall approve or deny an application for a parcel map for an urban lot split ministerially without discretionary review."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(b)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(b)(1)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "An application for an urban lot split shall be considered and approved or denied within 60 days from the date the local agency receives a completed application."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(b)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(b)(1)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "shall not impose regulations that require dedications of rights-of-way or the construction of offsite improvements for the parcels being created as a condition of issuing a parcel map for an urban lot split pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "shall not impose objective zoning standards, objective subdivision standards, and objective design review standards that would have the effect of physically precluding the construction of two units on either of the resulting parcels or that would result in a unit size of less than 800 square feet."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(c)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "in all other circumstances not described in subparagraph (A), a local agency may require a setback of up to four feet from the side and rear lot lines."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(c)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(c)(3)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "shall not require, as a condition for ministerial approval of a parcel map application for the creation of an urban lot split, the correction of nonconforming zoning conditions."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(i) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(i) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "A local agency shall require that a rental of any unit created pursuant to this section be for a term longer than 30 days."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(h) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  "a local agency shall not be required to permit more than two units on a parcel created through the exercise of the authority contained within this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(j)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(j)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66411.7(b)(1)(A)-(B), (b)(3), (c)(2)-(3), (h), and (j)(1), as currently in effect. It is one state's statute. One quoted passage below (the setback rule) is drawn from source text in which the HTML places a line-wrap between the words "local" and "agency"; that mid-word line-wrap whitespace is a source-formatting artifact and has been normalized to a single space in the quotation, not a substantive correction. This clause covers the development-standards, dedication/offsite-improvement, timeline, rental-term, and unit-cap rules together for concision; it does not separately quote every subdivision cited, and it does not determine whether a specific ordinance's standards, a specific application's completeness, or a specific parcel's actual unit count in fact comply with these provisions.

THE CALIFORNIA COASTAL ACT IS NOT SUPERSEDED
Neither the two-unit-development statute nor the urban-lot-split statute supersedes, alters, or lessens the effect of the California Coastal Act of 1976. Both statutes carve out one specific exception from that general preservation of the Coastal Act: a local agency is not required to hold public hearings for coastal development permit applications for a housing development or urban lot split approved under these particular statutes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Nothing in this section shall be construed to supersede or in any way alter or lessen the effect or application of the California Coastal Act of 1976 (Division 20 (commencing with Section 30000) of the Public Resources Code), except that the local agency shall not be required to hold public hearings for coastal development permit applications for a housing development pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 65852.21(k) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 65852.21(k) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65852.21.)
  "Nothing in this section shall be construed to supersede or in any way alter or lessen the effect or application of the California Coastal Act of 1976 (Division 20 (commencing with Section 30000) of the Public Resources Code), except that the local agency shall not be required to hold public hearings for coastal development permit applications for urban lot splits pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 66411.7(n) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 66411.7(n) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66411.7.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (in fact, the same operative language appearing in two separate California Government Code sections), used as evidence of how California's SB 9 ministerial-approval statutes interact with its distinct coastal-management statute -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific coastal parcel, and most states have no comparable statewide coastal-development permitting regime to compare against. The two citations below are drawn from two different, independently numbered statutory sections (65852.21(k) and 66411.7(n)) that happen to contain substantively identical language, rather than from a single source repeated twice. This clause does not describe the substantive requirements of the California Coastal Act itself, including what activity constitutes "development" requiring a coastal development permit -- a topic addressed in a separate clause of this corpus's Coastal Development Permit Requirement Information Sheet -- and it does not determine whether a specific parcel is in fact within the coastal zone or subject to the Coastal Act at all.

SB 9 TWO-UNIT HOUSING DEVELOPMENT / URBAN LOT SPLIT — PROJECT INFORMATION

This sheet identifies the property, the owner, and the local agency for reference in connection with a two-unit housing development or urban lot split application. It states facts for identification purposes only; it does not itself constitute or substitute for the application that must be submitted to, and acted on by, the local agency, and it does not determine whether the proposed development or lot split qualifies for ministerial approval under any particular provision of Government Code section 65852.21 or 66411.7.

California law requires a local agency to consider a proposed housing development containing no more than two residential units within a single-family residential zone ministerially -- without discretionary review or a hearing -- if the development meets a defined set of statutory requirements. One of those requirements is a location condition: the parcel must be located within a city whose boundaries include some portion of an urbanized area or urban cluster (as the United States Census Bureau designates those areas), or, for an unincorporated area, the parcel must lie wholly within the boundaries of such an urbanized area or urban cluster. A separate requirement cross-references specific parcel-eligibility criteria drawn from a different housing-streamlining statute (Government Code section 65913.4, as it read on September 16, 2021).

expectedJSON.body: California law excludes certain categories of existing housing from eligibility for the two-unit ministerial-approval pathway. Notwithstanding any provision of the statute or any local law, the proposed development may not require demolition or alteration of housing subject to a recorded covenant, ordinance, or law restricting rents to levels affordable to moderate-, low-, or very-low-income persons and families; housing subject to any form of rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police power; or housing that has been occupied by a tenant within the last three years. Separately, the parcel is ineligible if its owner has exercised rights under the Ellis Act (Government Code section 7060 et seq.) to withdraw residential accommodations from rent or lease within the 15 years before the development proponent submits its application. The development is also ineligible if it is located in a contributing structure within a historic district on the State Historic Resources Inventory (or a historic property or district under a city or county ordinance), or on a parcel individually listed as a historical resource on that inventory or individually designated as a city or county landmark.

expectedJSON.body: California law requires a local agency to ministerially approve, without discretionary review, a parcel map for an urban lot split if the map meets a defined set of statutory requirements. The parcel map must subdivide an existing parcel into no more than two new parcels of approximately equal lot area, with neither resulting parcel smaller than 40 percent of the original parcel's lot area, and both resulting parcels must be no smaller than 1,200 square feet, unless a local agency has adopted an ordinance permitting a smaller minimum lot size. The parcel being subdivided must be located within a single-family residential zone and, as with a two-unit development, within a city whose boundaries include some portion of an urbanized area or urban cluster (or, for an unincorporated area, wholly within such an area) as the United States Census Bureau designates it.

A local agency may not impose regulations requiring dedication of rights-of-way or construction of offsite improvements as a condition of an urban-lot-split parcel map, and it may not require correction of nonconforming zoning conditions as a condition of ministerial approval. A local agency must also require that a rental of any unit created under this section be for a term longer than 30 days. Finally, notwithstanding several other statutes governing two-unit developments, density bonuses, and accessory dwelling units, a local agency is not required to permit more than two units on a parcel created through an urban lot split.
